In the small Accra office, the hiring panel had just finished its fourth interview of the day. Mr Boateng, who had run recruitment for fifteen years, closed his folder. "That one's a no. I can tell in five minutes."
Kwame, the team lead and newest on the panel, had noticed something. Two of Mr Boateng's "tell in five minutes" hires from last year were now among the best on the team; two others had left within months. Nobody had ever tracked which was which.
"I don't doubt your read," he said carefully. "But could we also score each candidate on the same five questions, and look back in a year?"
Rania from HR nodded. "We've never checked how our gut calls turned out."
Mr Boateng grunted, then picked up the score sheet.

qa.q: How many years had Mr Boateng run recruitment?
qa.a: Fifteen years.

qa.q: Why did Kwame speak 'carefully' to Mr Boateng?
qa.a: He respected the man's experience and didn't want to insult him, while still believing gut calls in hiring needed checking.

qa.q: What did Kwame suggest, and why does it suit hiring?
qa.a: Scoring every candidate on the same five questions and looking back in a year, because hiring gives slow, mixed feedback that experience alone doesn't sharpen.

qa.q: How might Mr Boateng feel about the score sheet?
qa.a: He may feel his skill is being doubted at first, but could also be curious to see how his calls actually turn out.

grounding: A team lead notices a veteran recruiter's confident gut calls have mixed results and asks for scored data alongside the gut.

passage:
At the Monday meeting of the finance team, Naveen tapped the whiteboard. "Trust me, the market turns up by Diwali. Twelve years I've done this; I can feel it."
Farhan, the senior analyst, had heard the same confidence last year, when the market went the other way. He didn't doubt that Naveen was sharp. But markets bounce around for a hundred reasons, and a forecast can be right by luck or wrong by luck; twelve years of that doesn't teach the way twelve years of fixing engines would.
After the meeting he opened a shared sheet. "Let's log every prediction the team makes, with a date and a reason, and see after a year how we did against a simple average."
Naveen raised an eyebrow. "You think my gut's wrong?"
"I think none of us know yet," Farhan said. "The sheet will tell us."

qa.q: By when did Naveen say the market would turn up?
qa.a: By Diwali.

qa.q: How does Farhan feel hearing Naveen's certainty about Diwali?
qa.a: Farhan feels doubtful but respectful; he doesn't question that Naveen is sharp, yet he heard the same confidence last year when the market went the other way.

qa.q: What does Farhan's shared sheet do that gut feeling can't?
qa.a: It records every prediction with a date and reason and compares the results with a simple average, giving the honest feedback the market itself doesn't.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel when Farhan says 'none of us know yet'?
qa.a: A bit challenged at first, but the reply includes Farhan too, so it may feel fair rather than personal.

grounding: A senior analyst notices a colleague's confident market forecasts in a noisy field and asks for logged predictions alongside gut feeling.

passage:
Subject: Our scholarship interviews

Hi Anand,

Something from yesterday's panel keeps bothering me. Three of our senior members said they could "just tell" which students would succeed. They were very sure, and they've done this for years.

But I went through the files from five years back. The students they were most excited about did no better, on average, than the ones they picked with doubts. Nobody had ever looked, so nobody knew.

It's not that they're poor judges. Guessing how a seventeen-year-old will do over five years is just noisy; you rarely find out, and when you do, luck is mixed in.

I'd like to propose we keep the interview but add a simple scoring sheet and a yearly check on how our picks did. Gut plus data, not gut alone.

Can we discuss on Thursday?

Tarun (Mr Chopra to the students, as they insist)

qa.q: How far back did Tarun look in the files?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: Why did the senior members feel so sure they could 'just tell'?
qa.a: Years of interviews gave the senior members a confident, proud sense of expertise, but nobody checked the results, so that confidence was never tested.

qa.q: What does Tarun propose, and why does it fit this kind of decision?
qa.a: Keeping interviews but adding a scoring sheet and a yearly check, because predicting students' futures gives slow, noisy feedback that gut alone can't learn from.

qa.q: How might the three senior members react to Tarun's proposal?
qa.a: Some might feel their judgement is being questioned, while others might welcome finally learning how their picks did.

grounding: A senior coordinator notices confident panel members whose picks never beat chance in a noisy field, and proposes data alongside gut feeling.

passage: Jahnavi, you're asking for your podcast what surprised me most as senior designer at an export house in Jaipur? Okay, it's Akash, your data bhaiya, talking. Every season, our buyers pick which block prints will sell in Europe. They're so sure. "This one will fly." "This one's dead." They've done it for twenty years. So last winter I got curious. I went back through three seasons of their picks and the actual sales sheets. Their hits and misses were almost a coin toss. Fashion abroad changes with a hundred things nobody here sees, and the sales figures arrive months later, mixed up with other reasons. Twenty years of guessing hadn't sharpened much. I didn't embarrass anyone. At the next meeting I just said, "Let's keep your pick, and also test twenty samples with two shops first." One buyer grumbled. The samples are selling differently from what anyone guessed.

qa.q: How many seasons of picks did Akash check?
qa.a: Three seasons of their picks and the actual sales sheets.

qa.q: What does Akash's quiet approach at the meeting suggest about his feelings toward the buyers?
qa.a: He seems to respect their experience and doesn't want to embarrass them, but he is also curious and doubtful, since the data showed their confidence wasn't matched by results.

qa.q: Which step did Akash add, and why does it suit this kind of decision?
qa.a: Testing twenty samples with two shops alongside the buyers' picks, because in a field with slow, mixed feedback, real data helps more than confident guesses.

qa.q: How might the grumbling buyer feel about the new sample test?
qa.a: The buyer may feel doubted or a little threatened after twenty years of trusting their own eye, even if the test is fair.

grounding: A senior notices experienced buyers confident in predicting sales, a field with noisy feedback, and asks for data alongside gut feeling.

passage: I'm Ganga, assistant coach at a football academy in Kozhikode. Every year our coaches pick the under-14 squad from a two-day trial, and they're proud of their eye. "That boy has something," they say, or "No fire in that one." Farhan, our head of scouting, is only twenty-six, but he did something none of the older coaches had tried. He dug out the trial lists from four years ago and checked who was still playing well now. Some "sure things" had quit. Some rejected boys were starring for other clubs. At the next trial he handed out simple sheets: sprint times, passes completed, how each boy responded after a mistake. "Write your gut feeling too," he told them. "We'll compare later." A couple of coaches muttered. I can't say what Farhan felt when they did. He just kept handing out the sheets.

qa.q: How many years back did Farhan look at the trial lists?
qa.a: Four years ago.

qa.q: Why might the older coaches have muttered at Farhan's sheets?
qa.a: They trust their eye and may feel their experience is being doubted, especially by someone younger.

qa.q: What made Farhan's approach to selection sensible?
qa.a: He kept the coaches' gut feelings but added simple measurements and a later comparison, because youth selection gives slow, noisy feedback.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Farhan's quiet persistence?
qa.a: Ganga admires what Farhan tried but admits not knowing what he felt, only seeing that he kept handing out the sheets calmly.

grounding: A colleague watches a young senior notice that confident trial selectors had a poor record, and ask for data alongside their gut.
